title: Cap. III Rat. 7: mere good pleasure would elect all equally disposed — Valentia
latin: Rat. 7. Si Deus praedestinaret ad gloriam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, et non ex praevisione operum, tum omnes ex aequo praedestinaret, quia omnes aeque dispositi sunt ad illud donum recipiendum. Nam si Deus non eligat homines quatenus praevidentur ut bene operantes, et in bonis operibus perseverantes, consequens est ut eligantur quatenus praesciuntur esse homines, vel peccatores: at hoc omnibus convenit; omnes ergo eligerentur. Habetur hoc argumentum apud Gregorium de Valentia, In 1. qu. 23.
pass_a: Reason 7. If God should predestine to glory from the mere good pleasure of his will, and not from foresight of works, then he would predestine all equally, because all are equally disposed to receive that gift. For if God does not elect men inasmuch as they are foreseen as well-working, and persevering in good works, it follows that they are elected inasmuch as they are foreknown to be men, or sinners: but this belongs to all; therefore all would be elected. This argument is found in Gregory of Valencia, On 1. q. 23.
pass_b: Rat. 7. If God predestined to glory from the mere good pleasure of his will and not from foresight of works, then he would predestine all alike, because all are equally disposed to receive that gift. For if he does not elect people as foreseen working well and persevering in good works, they must be elected as foreknown to be human beings or sinners — which belongs to all; so all would be elected. So argues Gregory of Valencia (In 1. q. 23).

lemmas.lemma: ex mero beneplacito / non praevisione operum
lemmas.gloss: mere good pleasure vs foresight of works

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7: Major fails — good pleasure may discriminate; none disposed to glory
latin: Sol. Vacillat Majoris consequentia. Neque enim sequitur, ut in quibus Deus agit ex mero suo beneplacito, semper aequaliter agere cum aequalibus teneatur: Imo e contra, quia agit ex beneplacito, potest discrimen facere in collatione suorum beneficiorum ubi nullum fuit discrimen in qualitatibus aut statu personarum. Quod autem affertur primo in loco ad confirmationem Majoris, scilicet Exclusa praescientia operum, omnes esse aeque dispositos ad donum electionis recipiendum, falso et imperite a Gregorio asseritur. Dicere debuisset omnes esse prorsus indispositos ad gloriam recipiendam, atque dispositos ad poenas gehennae subeundas. Quae enim dispositio, ut eligatur ad gloriam, in illo reperitur, qui naturae irae filius, et labe originali contaminatus consideratur?
pass_a: Solution. The Major's consequence wavers. For it does not follow that in those things in which God acts from his mere good pleasure, he is always bound to act equally with equals: Nay on the contrary, because he acts from good pleasure, he can make a difference in the conferring of his benefits where there was no difference in the qualities or state of the persons. But what is brought first in place for confirmation of the Major, namely that with foresight of works excluded, all are equally disposed to receive the gift of election, is falsely and unskillfully asserted by Gregory. He ought to have said that all are altogether undisposed to receive glory, and disposed to undergo the pains of hell. For what disposition, that he be elected to glory, is found in him who is considered a child of wrath by nature, and contaminated with original stain?
pass_b: Sol. The Major's consequence fails. It does not follow that wherever God acts from mere good pleasure he must always deal equally with equals — on the contrary, because he acts from good pleasure he can discriminate in conferring his gifts where there was no difference in persons' qualities or state. And Gregory's first support for the Major — that with foresight of works excluded all are equally disposed to receive election — is false and unskillful. He should have said all are wholly undisposed to receive glory and disposed to undergo hell's pains. What disposition for election to glory is found in one reckoned a child of wrath by nature, stained with original corruption?

lemmas.gloss: undisposed to glory; child of wrath

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7: Lazarus analogy — no duty to raise all equally
latin: Sicuti ergo inepta esset haec argumentatio, Si Christus in terris agens mortuum Lazarum resuscitavit ad vitam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, et non ex praevisione alicujus cooperationis ex parte Lazari, tum omnes mortuos ex aequo resuscitasset, quia omnes aeque dispositi fuerant ad hoc donum resuscitationis recipiendum; sic etiam et prior illa Gregorii invalida et inepta est; quia supponit obligationem in Deo, ut quoties agit ex beneplacito, agat pariter cum paribus; et quia ponit communem dispositionem in hominibus ad recipiendum donum electionis, qui sunt communiter dispositi ad recipiendam poenam damnationis.
pass_a: Just as therefore this argumentation would be inept: If Christ acting on earth raised dead Lazarus to life from the mere good pleasure of his will, and not from foresight of any cooperation on Lazarus's part, then he would have raised all the dead equally, because all had been equally disposed to receive this gift of resuscitation; so also that prior [argument] of Gregory is invalid and inept; because it assumes an obligation in God, that as often as he acts from good pleasure, he act alike with equals; and because it posits a common disposition in human beings to receive the gift of election, who are commonly disposed to receive the punishment of damnation.
pass_b: Just as it would be inept to argue: if Christ on earth raised dead Lazarus from mere good pleasure of his will, not from foresight of any cooperation on Lazarus's part, then he would have raised all the dead alike, because all were equally disposed to receive that gift of raising — so Gregory's prior argument is invalid and inept. It assumes God is bound, whenever he acts from good pleasure, to deal alike with equals; and it posits a common disposition to receive election in people who are commonly disposed to receive damnation's punishment.

lemmas.gloss: no duty to treat equals alike from good pleasure

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7: not elect as man/sinner; gratis dilecti; Aquinas dilectio/electio
latin: Quod autem attinet ad posteriorem partem confirmationis, ubi colligit Gregorius, Si homines non eligantur ad gloriam quatenus praevisi sunt bene operantes, tum electi sunt quatenus praesciuntur homines, vel quatenus peccatores; quod cum omnibus convenit, electio etiam omnibus conveniret; haec etiam argumentatio frivola est. Nam cum recte Philosophi statuunt, Quod convenit rei quatenus tali, convenit omni tali, certum est electionem Dei non cadere in hominem quatenus hominem, neque in peccatorem quatenus peccatorem, quia ex eventu liquet, non omnibus hominibus, neque omnibus peccatoribus contingere ut eligantur. Negamus ergo illam distinctionem, Aut Deus eligit homines quatenus praevidentur cooperaturi gratiae suae, aut quatenus praesciuntur ut homines vel peccatores, et dicimus Deum eligere homines quatenus sibi prae aliis fuerunt gratis dilecti. Siquis porro quaerat, Cur hi prae aliis gratis dilecti? ridicula quaestio est: nam prima causa voluntatis Divinae in diffusione suorum bonorum, est ipsa voluntas; cujus ulterior causa non est indaganda. Non male Aquinas; Part. 1. qu. 23. art. 4. Praedestinatio aliquorum in salutem aeternam praesupponit secundum rationem quod Deus velit eorum salutem. Ad quod pertinet Electio et Dilectio: Dilectio quidem, in quantum vult eis hoc bonum salutis aeternae; Electio autem, in quantum hoc bonum eis vult prae aliis. Et haec voluntas Dei qua vult bonum alicui diligendo, est causa quod illud bonum ab eo prae aliis habeatur. Et sic patet, quod Dilectio praesupponitur Electioni, et Electio praedestinationi. Hactenus ille.
pass_a: But as for what pertains to the latter part of the confirmation, where Gregory gathers: If men are not elected to glory inasmuch as they are foreseen well-working, then they are elected inasmuch as they are foreknown as men, or inasmuch as sinners; which since it belongs to all, election also would belong to all; this argumentation also is frivolous. For since the Philosophers rightly establish, What belongs to a thing inasmuch as such, belongs to every such, it is certain that God's election does not fall upon a human being inasmuch as a human being, nor upon a sinner inasmuch as a sinner, because from the event it is clear that it does not happen to all human beings, nor to all sinners, that they be elected. We therefore deny that distinction, Either God elects men inasmuch as they are foreseen about to cooperate with his grace, or inasmuch as they are foreknown as men or sinners, and we say that God elects men inasmuch as they were freely loved by him before others. If anyone further asks, Why these freely loved before others? the question is ridiculous: for the first cause of the divine will in the diffusion of its goods is the will itself; whose further cause is not to be sought. Not badly Aquinas; Part 1 q. 23 art. 4. Predestination of some unto eternal salvation presupposes according to reason that God wills their salvation. To which belong Election and Love: Love indeed, inasmuch as he wills them this good of eternal salvation; but Election, inasmuch as he wills them this good before others. And this will of God by which he wills a good to someone by loving is the cause that that good is had from him before others. And so it is clear that Love is presupposed to Election, and Election to predestination. Thus far he.
pass_b: As for Gregory's second support — if people are not elected to glory as foreseen working well, then they are elected as foreknown humans or as sinners, and since that belongs to all, election would belong to all — that too is frivolous. Philosophers rightly hold that what belongs to a thing as such belongs to every such; yet God's election does not fall on a person as human, nor on a sinner as sinner, because the event shows not all humans and not all sinners are elected. So we deny the fork Either God elects as foreseen cooperators with his grace, or as foreknown humans/sinners — and say he elects people as freely loved by him ahead of others. Why these freely loved ahead of others? A ridiculous question: the first cause of the divine will in pouring out its goods is the will itself; no further cause is to be hunted. Aquinas is not wrong (ST I q.23 a.4): predestination of some to eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation. To that belong Love and Election: Love, inasmuch as he wills them this good of eternal salvation; Election, inasmuch as he wills them that good ahead of others. And that willing-by-loving is why they have the good from him ahead of others. So Love is presupposed to Election, and Election to predestination. So far Aquinas.

lemmas.gloss: election not as human or as sinner

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7 close: gratuitous affection first; Romans 9:12; Ephesians 1:5
latin: Ex quibus videtis, non praescientiam humanae cooperationis, sed gratuitum affectum Dei solummodo praesupponi ut antecedens ad electionem et praedestinationem singularum personarum. Quod Apostolus illustravit in illo celeberrimo exemplo Jacobi et Esavi, quod proponitur Rom. ix. 12. Et etiam disertis verbis expressit Ephes. i. 5. Qui praedestinavit nos, quos adoptaret in filios per Jesum Christum in sese, pro beneplacito affatus voluntatis suae. Atque hic huic argumento factum est satis.
pass_a: From which you see that not foresight of human cooperation, but the gratuitous affection of God alone is presupposed as antecedent to the election and predestination of singular persons. Which the Apostle illustrated in that most celebrated example of Jacob and Esau, which is set forth in Romans 9:12. And he also expressed it in clear words in Ephesians 1:5. Who predestined us, whom he would adopt as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the good pleasure of the utterance of his will. And here enough has been done for this argument.
pass_b: From this you see: not foresight of human cooperation, but God's gratuitous affection alone is presupposed as antecedent to the election and predestination of particular persons. The Apostle illustrated it in that famous example of Jacob and Esau (Romans 9:12), and said it in plain words in Ephesians 1:5: who predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will. And here enough for this argument.

lemmas.gloss: predestined for adoption by good pleasure
